terms.definition: An AWS service that automatically manages a collection of EC2 instances, adding more when demand rises (scale out) and removing them when demand drops (scale in), within defined minimum and maximum limits.
terms.example: Like a coffee shop chain that automatically opens more branches on busy days and closes extras when traffic is low.

terms.definition: A reusable configuration blueprint that tells ASG what kind of EC2 instance to create — including AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, and user data.
terms.example: Like a franchise manual that ensures every new branch has the same equipment setup.

terms.definition: The target number of EC2 instances the ASG tries to maintain at all times. ASG starts with this count and adjusts based on scaling policies.
terms.example: You set Desired = 3, so ASG always tries to keep exactly 3 instances running.

terms.definition: The lowest number of EC2 instances ASG will ever maintain. Even during zero traffic, ASG will never go below this number.
terms.example: Minimum = 2 means you always have at least 2 instances for baseline availability.

terms.definition: The highest number of EC2 instances ASG will ever create. Even during a massive traffic spike, ASG won't exceed this limit.
terms.example: Maximum = 6 caps your spending — you'll never accidentally spin up 100 instances.

terms.definition: An ASG scaling policy that automatically adjusts capacity to keep a specific CloudWatch metric at a target value. AWS's recommended policy for most workloads.
terms.example: Like a thermostat — you set 'keep CPU at 50%' and ASG handles everything else automatically.

terms.definition: An ASG scaling policy that adds or removes different numbers of instances based on how far a metric exceeds a threshold — proportional scaling steps.
terms.example: CPU 60-70% → add 1 instance; CPU 70-90% → add 2 instances; CPU >90% → add 3 instances.

terms.definition: An ASG scaling policy that performs a single fixed scaling action when a CloudWatch alarm fires, then waits for a cooldown period before acting again.
terms.example: When CPU > 70%, add 1 instance. Then wait 300 seconds before checking again.

terms.definition: An ASG scaling policy that uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively provisions capacity before anticipated demand spikes.
terms.example: If traffic spikes every Monday at 9 AM, Predictive Scaling adds instances at 8:45 AM automatically.

terms.definition: An ASG scaling policy that changes capacity at specific, pre-defined times using a cron schedule.
terms.example: Every Friday 5 PM: scale up to 10. Every Monday 6 AM: scale down to 3.

terms.definition: Manually changing the desired capacity of an ASG. ASG then adds or removes instances to match the number you set.
terms.example: You go to the console and type 'Desired Capacity = 5'. ASG adds 2 instances (from 3 to 5).

terms.definition: A Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancer that distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets and supports advanced routing based on URL path, host, header, and more.
terms.example: Like a hotel concierge who directs guests to different departments based on what they need.

terms.definition: A process on an ALB that checks for incoming connection requests on a specific port and protocol, then routes them based on configured rules.
terms.example: An ALB listener on port 80 waits for HTTP requests and applies rules to decide where to send each one.

terms.definition: A condition-and-action pair configured on an ALB Listener. When a request matches the condition, the action (e.g., forward to Target Group) is executed.
terms.example: Rule: IF path is /api/* THEN forward to API Target Group.

terms.definition: A logical grouping of targets (EC2 instances, Lambda functions, IP addresses, or containers) that ALB routes traffic to. Each Target Group has its own health check configuration.
terms.example: Like a team of workers — ALB sends tasks to the whole team, and the team members (EC2 instances) handle them.

terms.definition: An ALB feature that forwards requests to different Target Groups based on the URL path in the HTTP request.
terms.example: Requests to /api/* go to the API backend. Requests to /images/* go to the media server.

terms.definition: An ALB feature that forwards requests to different Target Groups based on the domain name (Host header) in the HTTP request.
terms.example: api.company.com → API Target Group; www.company.com → Web Target Group. One ALB handles both.

terms.definition: A periodic test that ALB sends to each registered target to verify it's healthy and able to serve traffic. Failed targets are removed from rotation.
terms.example: ALB sends GET / to each EC2 instance every 30 seconds. If the instance returns 500, it's marked unhealthy.

terms.definition: A component in a system that, if it fails, causes the entire system to stop working. Vertical scaling (one big server) creates a SPOF.
terms.example: A coffee shop with only one kitchen — if the kitchen breaks, the whole shop stops. Multiple shops eliminate this.

terms.definition: Adding more instances (scale out) to distribute load instead of making one instance bigger. AWS-recommended approach because it eliminates single points of failure.
terms.example: Instead of upgrading from 1 to a bigger server, you run 3 medium servers. If one fails, the other 2 keep running.

terms.definition: Upgrading a single server to a more powerful machine (more CPU, RAM). Simple but creates a single point of failure and has hardware limits.
terms.example: Upgrading an EC2 instance from t2.micro to t2.xlarge for more CPU and memory.

terms.definition: When enabled on an ASG, this type of health check uses ALB's application-level results to determine instance health — not just EC2 OS checks.
terms.example: Even if the EC2 OS is running fine, if Apache crashes, ELB health check fails → ASG replaces the instance.

terms.definition: An ALB feature (enabled by default) that allows each ALB node to distribute traffic to all registered targets across all enabled AZs, not just its own.
terms.example: ALB node in AZ-A can send traffic to EC2 instances in AZ-B, ensuring even distribution even if AZ-A has fewer instances.

terms.definition: The time ALB waits for in-flight requests to complete before fully deregistering a target. Default is 300 seconds.
terms.example: ASG scales in and wants to terminate an instance. ALB waits for any active requests on that instance to finish (up to 300s) before deregistering and allowing termination.

terms.definition: Adding more instances to an ASG in response to increased demand. The 'horizontal' direction of scaling — making the fleet wider.
terms.example: Traffic spikes on Black Friday → ASG scale out: 3 instances → 6 instances.

terms.definition: Removing instances from an ASG when demand decreases, to save cost. The reverse of scale out.
terms.example: Traffic drops at night → ASG scale in: 6 instances → 2 instances (minimum).
